analysis.one_liner: Bars group health plans from cutting retirees' health benefits after they retire.
analysis.headline: The bill to protect retiree health benefits won 60 cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend ERISA, the federal law governing employer benefits, to prohibit employer group health plans from canceling, cutting, or raising the out-of-pocket costs of health benefits for retirees after the date they retired. It would also require plans to offer to restore benefits that had already been taken away from current retirees after their retirement, with a hardship waiver process for struggling employers backed by a federal loan-guarantee program capped at $5 billion. Violations would carry civil penalties enforced by the Secretary of Labor.
analysis.who_benefits: Current retirees whose health benefits were reduced or canceled after they retired could get them restored, and future retirees would be shielded from post-retirement benefit cuts that they had counted on for life. The bill's findings describe retirees who lost group coverage and could not replace it because of preexisting conditions, sometimes depleting their life savings.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any group health plan, through amendment or otherwise, from reducing benefits provided to a retired participant after their retirement date, including canceling benefits, increasing out-of-pocket costs, or reducing access to services; plan provisions purporting to allow such cuts are void as against public policy [S3].

Requires plan sponsors to offer benefit restoration to retired participants whose benefits were reduced after their retirement date, with written notice itemizing the value of each benefit to be restored and a deadline for restoration within three years of enactment [S3].

Allows the Secretary of Labor to waive or vary restoration requirements only where compliance would be adverse to participants in the aggregate, not administratively feasible, and would cause substantial business hardship, and bars waivers for sponsors that could have transferred excess pension assets to fund retiree health or that maintain well-funded pension plans while denying cost-of-living adjustments [S3].

Establishes an Emergency Retiree Health Loan Guarantee Program, backed by $200 million in appropriations, to guarantee loans from private banks so struggling plan sponsors can meet their restoration obligations, with guarantees capped at $5 billion overall and $5 million per sponsor [S3].

Empowers the Secretary of Labor to assess civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation per affected participant or beneficiary, and lets participants take part in proceedings on waiver applications by their plan sponsor [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor retiree group health plans would bear the cost of keeping benefits at retirement levels and, where cuts already occurred, of restoring them. Struggling sponsors could seek hardship waivers or federally guaranteed loans, and sponsors receiving guarantees would pay a 0.5 percent fee plus loan interest; taxpayers would back up to $5 billion in guarantees and fund the program's administration.

drawbacks.text: Restoring previously canceled benefits would impose new, retroactive costs on plan sponsors, and the bill contemplates that compliance could necessitate 'substantial future reductions in health benefits' for active participants or a 'substantial decline in employment' at the sponsor [S3].

The loan-guarantee program authorizes up to $5 billion in federal guarantees and $200 million in appropriations to help employers finance their restoration obligations, so taxpayers would share the risk if sponsors could not repay [S3].
Plans with fewer than 100 participants are entirely exempt, and the Secretary may waive requirements for hardship, so the protection is not universal [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For retirees who lost promised health coverage after retirement — often unable to buy substitute insurance because of preexisting conditions — the benefit is substantial and the bill's waiver standards are designed to spare genuinely distressed employers. The main honest cost is borne by employers, some of which would pass it to active workers or jobs, plus a modest federal exposure through loan guarantees. The bill was never taken up, so no such tradeoff was ever tested or scored publicly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions subcommittee, and died there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the bill on March 5, 2009, joined by Reps. George Miller and Robert Andrews, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].
On April 29, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where it remained for the rest of the 111th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 59 cosponsors, 58 House Democrats and 1 House Republican, but the committee never held a hearing or markup and the bill never reached the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that sponsor retiree group health plans are better off, since they avoided a federal obligation to maintain or restore retiree benefits they had cut. Retirees whose benefits were reduced after retirement got no relief.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic: 58 of the 59 cosponsors were House Democrats, with a single House Republican joining.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring retiree group health plans
industries.note: The bill would bar them from cutting retiree health benefits after retirement and require restoration of benefits already cut, a direct cost to them; some might offset it against active workers or employment. Struggling sponsors could seek hardship waivers or federally guaranteed loans.
The bill would create a federally guaranteed loan market — up to $5 billion — for lenders making retiree-health loans to plan sponsors, with a 0.5 percent fee to Treasury and GAO audit rights.
